featured.name: Start Here
featured.blurb: {COUNT} books is a lot to walk into. These five are the way in: the first book of each series, and the flagship of the restored classics line. Start at whichever one sounds like yours and follow the shelf from there.

books.why: Book one of Things Left Open. A ledger that does not balance, and a stranger already willing to pay too much for it.
Book one of The Marjorie Corey Files. Three women inherit a coffee shop and sixty years of what the town agreed not to say.
Book one of The Keystone Cycle. Literary fiction built on the documented record.
Book one of The Gadget Sandbox Chronicles, for young builders and tinkerers.
The flagship of the restored classics line. Bierce and Chambers, annotated, the mythos before Lovecraft.

bestseller.name: The King in Yellow
bestseller.blurb: The book readers find on their own, with no funnel pointing at it. Chambers published it in 1895 and never once lets you read the cursed play at its centre. You only ever meet the people it has already ruined. Lovecraft built on this book, and a century later True Detective sent a new generation looking for Carcosa and the Yellow Sign without knowing where either came from.
bestseller.connected_blurb: The Yellow Sign did not begin with Chambers and it did not end with him. {N} more restored editions trace the line, from the Bierce tales he borrowed his names from to the English weird stories that carried the same dread forward. Each one is annotated for this edition.

connected.why: The Bierce stories Chambers took Carcosa and Hali from, printed in publication order beside the four Yellow Sign tales, so the borrowing reads as a sequence rather than a rumour.
Chambers went back to the weird two years later. Breton legend, buried violence, and the same trick of showing you the aftermath instead of the thing itself.
Machen, 1894. A surgical experiment on a young woman, and the quiet ruin it leaves behind for decades. The English weird tale at its most influential.
Blackwood, 1907. Two men camped on an island in the Danube, and a place that has noticed them. Nothing is ever shown, which is precisely the point.

sections.name: Things Left Open
sections.blurb: Five standalone but connected novels following different heirs across the Greek diaspora. Read any one alone. They are richest in order.

books.hook: A grandmother dies and leaves Marina a ledger that does not balance, and a stranger is already willing to pay far too much for it.

sections.name: The Marjorie Corey Files
sections.blurb: Three women co-inherit the Ginger Mae Coffee Shop on Patchogu Island, off the North Carolina Outer Banks, and inherit sixty years of what the town agreed not to say out loud.

books.hook: A JFK assassination thread and a secret the island kept for sixty years.

sections.name: The Keystone Cycle
sections.blurb: Five Greek diaspora teenagers share a converted sponge merchant's house on Kalymnos, then go on to the places their families left: Tarpon Springs, Darwin, Sfax, Alexandria, Broome. Each of them turns up a document there first. Each book stands alone. They read richer as a cycle.

sections.name: The Gadget Sandbox Chronicles
sections.blurb: Six friends, six worlds inside a building sandbox, and one new rule for building, testing, and saving in each book. This is where Captain Cubemelon's crew starts, and where every build begins. Ages 10 to 14.

sections.name: The Glitch Blocks
sections.blurb: The same crew, after the six worlds are linked and the rules are earned. Fourteen small glitches start flickering between the doors, changing which one opens where. They cannot be fought, only understood. Some of them turn out to be frightened. Ages 8 to 12.

sections.name: Standalone Novels
sections.blurb: A missing sister in a mountain town. A wealth firm with six months to name a successor. A night photographer who only ever watched. An encrypted ledger going back four centuries. They share nothing but the moment somebody decides not to look away.

excerpt.name: The Sponge Cache
excerpt.sub: Things Left Open, Book One. Chapter One, The Funeral.
excerpt.cta: That is the first scene. The next five chapters are yours free, as EPUB and PDF.
excerpt._note: VERBATIM from Manuscript-Clean-Export/Book-1-The-Sponge-Cache-manuscript.md. This is his own copyrighted prose, so it is safe to publish, and it is an ORIGINAL WORK, so it must NEVER be altered: do not restyle punctuation, do not 'fix' anything. It happens to contain no em dashes, en dashes or ellipses, so it passes the build guard unchanged. If a future excerpt DOES contain them, preserve the text and exempt it from the guard. Never edit the work to satisfy a linter.
paragraphs: Marina counted nine mourners who still spoke Alexandrian Greek and seventeen who did not. The funeral was small. Her grandmother had wanted it small, and the people who came spoke either the Alexandrian Eudoxia had carried for sixty-five years in Athens or the Athenian her daughter had refused to inherit and refused to replace. Anastasia received condolences without correcting anyone's Greek. Marina, who had spent the morning cataloguing the mourners by their accents because it was the only thing she could think to do, stood a half step behind her mother and held her gloves.

The cemetery was on the south slope of the city. The Greek-Egyptian section was a small plot at the back, where the cypresses thinned and the city spread out toward Piraeus in the afternoon light. Eudoxia had picked the plot twenty years ago, paid for it in francs converted on a holiday, and told no one until the paperwork had to be witnessed. That was Eudoxia. Marina had organized the witnesses herself. She had been twenty-four, a graduate student, and her grandmother had said this is the kind of thing I prefer to do while I can still sign my own name.

The priest read in Greek with a slight Cypriot inflection. Eudoxia had liked him because he did not pretend to be Alexandrian. The reading was short. Eudoxia had wanted the prayers and not the speeches, and the family had honored it. No one stood to say anything about who she was. Marina had been grateful for it during the service and was grateful for it again now, watching the small line of mourners form to embrace her mother. She would not have known what to say. She had spent a career writing about the women her grandmother had been one of, and had not known how to be in a room of them as a granddaughter.

Anastasia stood very straight. The last of the early-autumn warmth still hung in the cypresses. A drop of sweat moved down the back of Anastasia's neck and Marina watched it without reaching to wipe it. Her mother would not have wanted her to. The line moved forward.

The woman who took Anastasia's hand was perhaps eighty. She wore a small dark hat with a veil and a thin gold cross. She did not introduce herself. Anastasia thanked her in formal Greek. The woman moved past Anastasia toward Marina and stopped in front of her and looked at her for long enough that Marina noticed Anastasia notice. The woman's hands were dry and careful when she took Marina's. She held them.
"I knew your grandmother in Alexandria," the woman said. "I am Lysandra Kallistos."
Lysandra did not release her hands. "There are some things she did not finish," she said. "Pragmata pou meinan anoichta. You will know what to do."

The Alexandrian Greek was perfect. The phrase was Eudoxia's phrase. Marina had heard her grandmother use it about a half-translated letter, about a sweater she had not finished, about a question Marina had asked her once at seventeen and that Eudoxia had refused to answer that day and had not returned to. Things left open. Marina did not move her hands.
"I do not know what you mean," she said.
